Context/Background:
Intraductal papillary neoplasms (IPNs),  including intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasms (IOPNs), and intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasms (ITPNs), are clinically detectable macroscopic non-invasive cyst-forming lesions, some of which progress to invasive pancreatic cancer. Proteins and glycoproteins have proven to be useful clinical biomarkers for classifying cyst-forming neoplasms in the pancreas.Here, we used proteomics and glycoproteomics to characterize a series of histologically and genetically well-characterized surgically resected IPNs, including IPMNs and IOPNs.

Our analysis included 69 IPNs (64 IPMNs and 5 IOPNs), 76 macro-dissected grossly normal duct tissues (NDs, with 32 of the 76 NDs coming from the same resection specimens as the IPNs), and 32 cyst fluid samples (22 from matched IPMN patients, 3 matched IOPN patients, 2 from unrelated IPMN patients, and 5 other cysts).
Prompt: Look at the differential genes between IPMN and ND samples, provide a summary of enriched pathways in IPMN compared to ND.

Introduction/Context  
The dataset (Wang_2025_Cancer_Cell_TableS2A.csv) reports proteomic differential expression (log2 FC and FDR) for 9,417 proteins comparing pancreatic IPMN lesions (n = 64) versus macro‐dissected normal ducts (ND, n = 76; 32 matched). Tissue source, histology, and assay platform (mass‐spectrometry proteomics/glycoproteomics) are specified; replicates and exact instrument details are not. Key DE signals include strong downregulation (negative NES) of translational machinery and pancreatic‐function proteins, and upregulation of immune, cytoskeletal, and EMT‐related pathways.

Interpretation  
IPMN lesions exhibit a pronounced suppression of translational and ribosomal biogenesis pathways, alongside downregulation of pancreas‐specific secretion and digestion proteins. In contrast, IPMNs upregulate immune/inflammatory modules (phagosome, interferon gamma, complement), cytoskeletal remodeling (actin organization, integrin signaling), and EMT programs. These shifts suggest a transition from a differentiated secretory phenotype toward a more mesenchymal, immune‐interacting state, consistent with cyst progression and early neoplastic remodeling.

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate key candidate markers (e.g., RPLP1, CELA3A, CFTR, FN1, MUC1) by targeted proteomics or immunohistochemistry.  
2. Assess whether immune pathway activation correlates with immune cell infiltration via spatial transcriptomics or IHC for CD45/HLA markers.  
3. Explore the functional impact of translational suppression on IPMN growth using polysome profiling.  
4. Determine if EMT activation in cyst fluid glycoproteome matches tissue‐based EMT signatures.
